source.title: Pretraining with hierarchical memories: separating long-tail and common knowledge
source.authors: Hadi Pouransari; D. Grangier; C. Thomas; Michael Kirchhof; O. Tuzel

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and table formatting are flattened, but the relevant text and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports downstream benchmark performance across model sizes and a token-per-parameter sweep for memory learning. It does not fit or test the stated dense-model power laws; the relevant measurements use different outcomes or training setups.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses dense-model scaling laws as background and says compute-optimal laws may not apply to memory learning. Its token-per-parameter experiment reports trends, not a fitted power law. Table 5 supplies comparable baseline downstream scores at three model sizes.
record.test_reason: The paper is about memory-augmented pretraining, not about scaling laws. It cites Hoffmann et al. only to say dense compute-optimal laws may not apply to memory learning. It fits no power law and makes no extrapolation or prediction. The baseline scores at 160M, 410M and 1.4B (Table 5) are reference points for the memory method, not a test of whether downstream performance is predictable from scale. Three monotonically rising points without any fitted or predictive relation cannot show V6's 'predictably'. The tokens-per-parameter sweep (Fig. 7) and the bank-size trends (Fig. 3d, 4a) concern memory parameters trained on a frozen anchor. That is a different construct from any version: not a dense model, not pretraining loss against N/D/C, and no power-law form is examined.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that small models with hierarchical parametric memories (about 10% fetched parameters) match regular models with roughly 2x the parameters on knowledge tasks. The authors also claim deployment and privacy benefits. Scaling laws for memory learning are left as future work, since dense compute-optimal laws may not apply.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies hierarchical parametric memories, downstream benchmarks, and memory-training tokens per parameter rather than fitting dense-model held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Memory-learning results vary with tokens per parameter in the tested frozen-anchor setup; the paper reports steadily improving specific-knowledge accuracy and Wiki-En perplexity as TPP increases.

fits_no_version.finding: For memory parameters trained on a frozen 160M anchor, specific-knowledge accuracy and Wiki-En perplexity improve steadily with memory tokens-per-parameter from about 1 to 312. Performance rises strictly with memory bank size and with fetched memory size (Fig. 3d, 4a, 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse, cluster-routed memory parameters keep improving with training tokens per memory parameter far beyond dense compute-optimal ratios; no functional form is established.

record.problems: The relevant memory-learning curves are shown in figures without extracted numerical values or fitted power laws. Downstream size comparisons report aggregate scores without uncertainty estimates and do not fit or validate quantitative predictions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the listed versions were omitted. Other memory-type, clustering, retrieval, and deployment comparisons do not test the stated scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No compute-optimal allocation; the paper states Chinchilla laws may not apply to memory learning.
Shape at fixed parameters is not tested for loss. The 410M-runtime anchor/memory split (Fig. 4b) varies depth together with memory, not shape alone.
No power-law form is examined for memory learning or other regimes.
No predictive relation between scale or loss and downstream scores.
No fitting choices or exponents are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V6' rests on three baseline sizes increasing in Table 5. These are reference points for the method, not a scaling test, so the label is removed. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out pretraining cross-entropy against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolations from small runs are compared with much larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or fitted compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
The paper does not test how depth, width, or architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count.

The paper varies training tokens per parameter for memory learning, but does not test whether the resulting curve has the same power-law form as dense pretraining. It does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling-law regimes.
Downstream scores are compared across model sizes, but the paper does not fit a predictive relationship to pretraining loss or establish a quantitative prediction rule.
No fitted exponents, fitting-method comparison, compute-optimal split, or curve-bending analysis is reported. The discussion only notes that dense-model laws may not apply to memory learning.
